READING

**The fixed cost that doesn't count**

Both courses carry the same GBP 27,072 learning-curve bill (10 technicians × ~28 excess remakes × GBP 96). That figure belongs in the background; it doesn't discriminate between the two options and I will set it aside.

---

**The two variable costs that do count**

*KIRKBANE's hard cost: GBP 44,000 overtime.*
This is not an estimate. It is a quoted, certain figure paid entirely in cash to hold output volume while quality is temporarily low. It does not reduce the remake rate—it only keeps unit count up. The practices still see the elevated remake rate; they just receive the same volume of work while seeing it.

*AVENSWOOD's variable cost: crossing remakes.*
The pilot produced 40 crossing remakes over 4 months with 2 technicians split across systems. I need to project that onto nine months of dual running with up to 9:1 splits at various stages.

The crossing-remake rate is most plausibly tied to the number of in-flight cases that span a system boundary. Each technician who crosses carries roughly 20 crossing remakes in the pilot (40 ÷ 2 technicians). Ten technicians crossing under AVENSWAVE would, on that basis, produce about 200 crossing remakes: 200 × GBP 96 = GBP 19,200.

That is the *pessimistic* end. In practice AVENSWOOD's waves are structured: wave 1 completes its 900-unit curve while wave 2 is onboarding, so the window in which a given practice has technicians on both systems simultaneously narrows as each wave matures. A mid-range estimate of 80–120 crossing remakes (GBP 7,680–GBP 11,520) is more probable, but I will use the pessimistic figure of GBP 19,200 to stress-test the case.

**Even under the pessimistic crossing-remake assumption, AVENSWOOD costs roughly GBP 25,000 less in direct variable outlay than KIRKBANE.**

| | KIRKBANE | AVENSWOOD (pessimistic) |
|---|---|---|
| Overtime | GBP 44,000 | GBP 0 |
| Crossing remakes | GBP 0 | GBP 19,200 |
| **Variable total** | **GBP 44,000** | **GBP 19,200** |

---

**The quality exposure to practices**

The financial gap already favours AVENSWOOD, but the quality picture reinforces it.

Under KIRKBANE all ten remaining technicians enter the steep part of the curve simultaneously. The blended lab-wide remake rate in the opening months calculates to roughly:

(2 technicians × 3.4%) + (10 technicians × 11.4%) ÷ 12 ≈ **10%**

That is more than three times the settled rate of 3.1%, and it hits all forty practices in the same month. Overtime preserves unit volume but it cannot hide a trebling of the remake rate from practices whose patients have booked appointments around expected delivery dates. A practice experiencing two or three consecutive remakes on different cases in the same month has no signal that this is temporary; from their side it looks like a lab-wide deterioration.

Under AVENSWOOD the worst-case blended rate (wave 1, three technicians at 11.4%, remainder at 3.1%) is:

(2 × 3.4%) + (3 × 11.4%) + (7 × 3.1%) ÷ 12 ≈ **5.2%**

That is a 2-percentage-point elevation, distributed unevenly across practices rather than landing on all forty simultaneously. A practice handling a single remake knows it is an isolated event, not a lab-wide signal.

---

**Dual libraries: the real management burden**

Running two shade libraries and two material libraries for nine months is real overhead. The pilot already proved the lab can do it for four months. Extending to nine requires discipline—version control on shade notes, clear assignment of which practice communicates with which system technicians—but it is not a structural impossibility. The lab has already built the muscle.

Under KIRKBANE the single-library benefit is real but is purchased at a price of GBP 44,000 plus the reputational exposure of simultaneous quality deterioration across all forty practices.

---

**Timeline adequacy**

AVENSWOOD completes on 2027-10-04. Kessendale loses support on 2028-06-30. That is nearly nine months of clean buffer. There is no timeline argument for KIRKBANE's speed.

---

**Risk asymmetry**

KIRKBANE concentrates risk: cost, quality, and practice impact all peak in the same window. If anything goes wrong (a technician struggles unusually, a key practice complains loudly, sickness among the ten at a critical month), the damage is widespread and synchronised.

AVENSWOOD distributes risk: at any point three-quarters of the bench is at par, providing a visible quality backstop and giving experienced technicians the capacity to support newer converts. Waves also act as a learning-improvement loop—if wave 1 surfaces unexpected problems (tool gaps, training gaps), wave 2 benefits from that discovery before it starts.

---

**Verdict**

AVENSWOOD saves at minimum GBP 25,000 in direct cost over the pessimistic scenario, shields forty practices from a simultaneous quality shock, maintains operational continuity with three-quarters of the bench at settled quality throughout, and finishes nine months before the hard deadline. The dual-library burden is real but manageable, and the crossing-remake risk is bounded and well under the cost of overtime.

CALL
  AVENSWOOD

GROUNDS
  The GBP 44,000 certain overtime cost of KIRKBANE exceeds even the most pessimistic estimate of AVENSWOOD's crossing-remake exposure by roughly GBP 25,000, and KIRKBANE additionally risks all forty practices simultaneously experiencing a trebling of the remake rate in the same month—a reputational concentration of harm that the graduated approach structurally avoids.
